body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Region banter for Dawn's Gate and the Howlers Pass: 7 short exchanges between two or three companions, spoken as the party walks about this place. There are no Narrator rows, no options and no replies. Every row is a companion talking to another companion, never to the player.

HOW IT WORKS. When the party comes into an area, now and then one exchange plays as a few lines of chat between companions who happen to be in the party, once each. Only two or three of the six are ever in the party, so each exchange stands alone, mentions nobody else and needs no setup. Each one below is about what is in front of the party in one place at one moment of the story. Banter is funny first; one line in an exchange may turn honest, never more. The chat is about the place: what it looks and smells like, what is odd or sad or silly in it, and how each companion's trade, habits and fears meet it.

RULES.
1. Each exchange is 4 to 6 SAY rows, each a companion's single line (one or two short sentences, under about 28 words), alternating naturally between the speakers; every speaker listed speaks at least once.
2. Use only the facts in the attached cast sheets and the "In front of them" facts of that exchange. The "Story now" line is everything the party knows of the story: a remark must never run ahead of it (name a villain, a fight or a result only if the Story now line does). Never state or hint at any companion's past or secret, and never say what anyone's debt is. No new named people, places or monsters.
3. Pet words and phrases: each companion's at most once in an exchange, and never in two consecutive lines. Companions call each other by first name.
4. No two exchanges may share a joke or a topic, and no line may repeat a line in a cast sheet. Spread the topics: do not make every exchange about the same kind of thing.
5. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks). No em dashes, semicolons, brackets, asterisks or stage directions. No game terms. Our own words.
AVOID in this region: Do not describe the monastery's rulers or what happens inside it. Kristoff Gruber is the innkeeper; name no other villager.

THE EXCHANGES (in this order):
EXCHANGE 1: Silas + Delphine (speaker ids: silas_vane, delphine_ravelle)
  Story now: The party has come down into Dawn's Gate, a dour mining village below the monastery.
  Talk about: its first look: what the party sees and smells on coming in.
  In front of them: Dawn's Gate: A dour mining village in the Howlers' foothills, below a monastery whose red windows are never dark. Slate roofs, soot, and a copper glow of lamps. Red banners with a golden rose are nailed on every door, and above the village, on its peak, a bell tower stands black against the stars. Parts of it: The square; Before the Briar; The mine hill; The smelter; The hill path; The Hunt's lodge; The river road; The mill stream. Things to see: The river road, and the village ahead; The village bell post; The hill path sign; The Hunt's notice; The village well; A mine adit, timbered and shut; The smelter, smoking; A heap of slag; An ore cart. People here: Toma Flint; Halka Wren; Dagny Voll; Ser Maric Dunmore; Pilgrim Quill.
EXCHANGE 2: Rook + Tobin (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, tobin_hayward)
  Story now: The party is in the Briar's taproom.
  In front of them: The Briar Public House: Kristoff Gruber's inn: a low taproom of black beams, a kitchen, a cellar stair and rooms above. A low room of black beams and hunters' coats on pegs. The bar is scarred, the fire is good and nobody sings. Parts of it: The taproom; The kitchen; The bar; The stair. Things to see: A board of Hunt notices; The taproom fire; Barrels of black beer; Hunters' coats on pegs; A golden rose nailed over the door; A pot of something that was a goat; Hanging meat and strings of onions; A bar stool; A taproom table. People here: Kristoff Gruber.
EXCHANGE 3: Lucan + Cordelia (speaker ids: lucan_houndstooth, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The party has gone down to the Briar's cellar. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  In front of them: The Briar's Cellar: A cool cellar of casks, and a false wall behind them. Casks, cold stone, and behind the third rack a wall that is newer than the rest. Parts of it: The cellar. Things to see: Casks of black beer; Stacked crates; Sacks of barley.
EXCHANGE 4: Silas + Lucan (speaker ids: silas_vane, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: The party is upstairs at the Briar, in the small rooms over the taproom. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  In front of them: The Briar, Upstairs: Four small rooms over the taproom. Four narrow rooms under the eaves, each with a bed, a hook and a window on the red-lit hill. Parts of it: The rooms. Things to see: A window on the hill; A traveller's chest.
EXCHANGE 5: Silas + Cordelia (speaker ids: silas_vane, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The party is climbing the Howlers Pass towards the monastery, whose red windows light the way.
  Talk about: its first look: what the party sees and smells on coming in.
  In front of them: The Howlers Pass: A winding climb through slate-grey mountains and a copse of dead trees, with the monastery's red windows lighting the way. The path climbs in long bends of loose slate. Dead trees lean over it. Above, bats stream out of a black tower and the red windows throw a lit road to the gates. Parts of it: The foot of the climb; The camp ground; Before the gate; The long bends. Things to see: The monastery gate, and its watch; The monastery on its peak; Bats streaming from the belfry; A pilgrims' cairn; A cold fire ring; A signpost: THE CRIMSON ROSE RECEIVES ALL; A dead tree; Loose slate.
EXCHANGE 6: Delphine + Lucan (speaker ids: delphine_ravelle, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: Renathyr is dead. The party is back in Dawn's Gate, which is quieter. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  Talk about: something different from the other exchange in this place: how it feels now.
  In front of them: Dawn's Gate: A dour mining village in the Howlers' foothills, below a monastery whose red windows are never dark. Slate roofs, soot, and a copper glow of lamps. Red banners with a golden rose are nailed on every door, and above the village, on its peak, a bell tower stands black against the stars. Parts of it: The square; Before the Briar; The mine hill; The smelter; The hill path; The Hunt's lodge; The river road; The mill stream. Things to see: The river road, and the village ahead; The village bell post; The hill path sign; The Hunt's notice; The village well; A mine adit, timbered and shut; The smelter, smoking; A heap of slag; An ore cart. People here: Toma Flint; Halka Wren; Dagny Voll; Ser Maric Dunmore; Pilgrim Quill.
EXCHANGE 7: Rook + Silas (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, silas_vane)
  Story now: Renathyr is dead. The party goes back down the pass.
  Talk about: something different from the other exchange in this place: how it feels now.
  In front of them: The Howlers Pass: A winding climb through slate-grey mountains and a copse of dead trees, with the monastery's red windows lighting the way. The path climbs in long bends of loose slate. Dead trees lean over it. Above, bats stream out of a black tower and the red windows throw a lit road to the gates. Parts of it: The foot of the climb; The camp ground; Before the gate; The long bends. Things to see: The monastery gate, and its watch; The monastery on its peak; Bats streaming from the belfry; A pilgrims' cairn; A cold fire ring; A signpost: THE CRIMSON ROSE RECEIVES ALL; A dead tree; Loose slate.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line:

EXCHANGE <number>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
...

Use the speaker ids exactly as given (for example SAY rook_coldwake: ...). Write exactly 7 EXCHANGE blocks, numbered 1 to 7, and nothing else.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write: `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-1.md` (the voice sheets and fact lists for Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward and Silas Vane) and `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-2.md` (the same for Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein).
result:
EXCHANGE 1
SAY delphine_ravelle: Soot on the cobbles and the same red rag nailed to every door, Silas. Whoever dressed this house had a heavy hand with the red paint.
SAY silas_vane: Look up the hill at those red windows, friend, because the management is clearly keeping an eye on the table. Even the smelter smoke tastes like copper stakes.
SAY delphine_ravelle: My Fool is pulling faces at that heap of slag, and he does not even have a nose to wrinkle. Mind the seams, darling, the ash gets into everything.
SAY silas_vane: Ash I can brush off my ribs, Delphine, it is the timbered mine adit that bothers me. When a town boards up its only living, the game is already rigged.

EXCHANGE 2
SAY tobin_hayward: Keep me three paces back from that hearth, Rook, the fire is drawing too fierce for dry burlap. At least Kristoff Gruber keeps his onions dry and his rafters clean of rot.
SAY rook_coldwake: Low beams are a hazard for a tall shield, Tobin, though the masonry round the chimney is sound enough. Quiet sort of shift when nobody in the taproom sings.
SAY tobin_hayward: That pot on the hob was a goat once, before someone boiled the sins right out of it. Still, the mice in my lapels are twitching for a crust.
SAY rook_coldwake: Let them have my share of the broth, then, and remind me to sigh before we go up the stair. A watchman looks unruly if he sits by a good fire without breathing.
SAY tobin_hayward: You breathe when you please, Rook, just do not let that brass knocker on your shield clack while I am shaking the beetles out of my head.

EXCHANGE 3
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Hush now, Cordelia, Barnaby has his nose to the flagstones by the third rack. He never points at casks of black beer unless the stonework itself is dishonest.
SAY cordelia_skein: Your spectral Pomeranian has an admirable eye for masonry, darling. The mortar behind those barrels is decades fresher than the cellar around it, and the air leaks right through.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Let me take a brief sniff by the barley sacks, if you please. Damp lime, bruised hops, and the distinct spoor of someone bricks could not keep out.
SAY cordelia_skein: My six eyes just clicked at the draught coming through that seam, Lucan. Do hold still while we pry it open, my pulse charts love a surprise.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Good heavens, I only hope whatever waits behind the false wall has better posture than the last specimen we cornered in the dark.

EXCHANGE 4
SAY silas_vane: Four narrow beds under the eaves and I do not even sleep, Lucan, so you can have my bolster for Barnaby. Just keep the window shut against that red glare on the hill.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: You are most gracious, Silas, though Barnaby prefers to curl beneath my coat on the floor hook. One clap of mountain thunder and he forgets he is a harbinger of dread.
SAY silas_vane: Better a dog that hides under a coat than a shadow that lags half a step behind your boots. Mine has been staring at that traveller's chest since we came up.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Do not let the red light rattle your cards, friend. If you must spend four hours in revelry tonight, perhaps we might play a quiet hand on the blanket.
SAY silas_vane: You are on, Lucan, provided the hound does not yip every time I palm an ace off the bottom.

EXCHANGE 5
SAY cordelia_skein: Read the signpost, Silas, the Crimson Rose receives all, which sounds delightfully thorough. With those bats streaming from the belfry, the pathology up here must be thriving.
SAY silas_vane: When a house puts out a welcome sign on a dead mountain, friend, check the fine print before you step through the gate. Even the wind through my ribs tastes like cold iron.
SAY cordelia_skein: Mind your footing on the loose slate, darling, I cannot calibrate my vials if I am catching you on every bend. Look how the red windows light the stone like an artery.
SAY silas_vane: My censer is swinging three inches wider than it should, Cordelia, and the dead trees are leaning in to watch the deal. House always wins, unless you burn the house.
SAY cordelia_skein: Then let us climb to the watch at the gate and see what sort of humours keep those lamps burning all night.

EXCHANGE 6
SAY delphine_ravelle: Renathyr is dead, Lucan, and yet the red windows up there are still staring down like cheap stage lights. At least the square has stopped holding its breath.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: The air by the village well is cleaner, if you please, more river water and less old blood in the soot. Even Barnaby is trotting past the bell post with his tail up.
SAY delphine_ravelle: My Fool had three puns ready for the smelter and he dropped every one of them on the hill path. When a town goes this quiet after the curtain falls, it gives my stitching a chill.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: They have lived under that black tower a very long time, Delphine. Give them an evening to learn that the dark on the peak no longer has teeth.

EXCHANGE 7
SAY rook_coldwake: Loose slate is worse coming down than going up, Silas, and the grade on these bends is five degrees past regulation. Mind the turf by that cold fire ring.
SAY silas_vane: Scratch one more chalk tally inside my ribs for Renathyr, Rook, and call the tab settled. Walking away from the table with all our bones is the best hand we will get.
SAY rook_coldwake: Look at the pilgrims' cairn by the dead tree, every stone stacked neat by folk who marched up to that gate. I should take a chalk rubbing for the ledger before we leave the foot of the climb.
SAY silas_vane: Leave the stones to the bats in the belfry, friend, the living down the hill have had enough of ledgers. Come on, I will remind you to breathe when we hit the river road.
SAY rook_coldwake: Fair enough, Silas. Settle down now, and keep your shadow on the path where I can see it.
